topic.title: Sketching the graphs of sin x, cos x and tan x
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. A trigonometric graph has opened an early question in every paper read: Summer 2018 Q3(a) (sine, 2 marks), Summer 2019 Q4(a) (cosine, 2), Summer 2022 Q4(a) (sine over a negative range, 1), Summer 2023 Q3(a) (cosine from -180 to 180, 2) and Summer 2025 Q2(a) (tangent, 1). The axes are printed for you and the wording is either Sketch the graph of or Complete the graph of, with the range written underneath. The marks are for the shape and for the scale or key points, one each. The part that follows almost always solves an equation on the same curve for 2 or 3 marks, and the readings are marked against the candidate's own graph, so an accurate sketch is paid for twice.
mustMemorise: Period 360° for sin and cos, 180° for tan
tan x has asymptotes at ±90° and ±270°; the curve never touches them
One smooth curve, and a scale on both axes
sin(180° − x) = sin x; cos(360° − x) = cos x; tan(x + 180°) = tan x
notOnThisSpec: Transformations of the three curves — the Teacher Guidance says sin 2x and cos(x - 30°) will not be asked
Radians: every angle in Unit 1 is measured in degrees
The reciprocal curves and any graph outside -360° ≤ x ≤ 360°
The sine rule and the cosine rule, which the Teacher Guidance excludes here
Amplitude as a variable quantity: with no stretches on this specification it is always 1

mustBeAbleTo: Draw y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x over any range inside -360° ≤ x ≤ 360°
Mark the five key points of the sine and cosine curves and write a scale on both axes
Draw the asymptotes of the tangent curve as dashed lines the curve never meets
State the period of each curve, and use it to continue a graph beyond the range drawn
Say why the greatest value of sin x and cos x is 1 and the least is −1
Draw a horizontal line across a curve and count how many solutions an equation has
Read a solution off a drawn curve to the accuracy the question allows
Use sin(180° − x) = sin x, cos(360° − x) = cos x and tan(x + 180°) = tan x to turn one angle into another
sheet.howExamined: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. A trigonometric graph has opened an early question in most papers: Summer 2018 Q3(a) (cosine from 0° to 360°, 2 marks), Summer 2019 Q4(a) (cosine from −90° to 360°), Summer 2022 Q4(a) (sine from −360° to 0°, 1), Summer 2023 Q3(a) (cosine from −180° to 180°, 2) and Summer 2025 Q2(a) (complete the tangent graph from −90° to 270°, 1). The axes are printed for you and the wording is Sketch the graph of or Complete the graph of, with the range written underneath. The marks are for the shape and for the scale or key points. The part that follows usually solves an equation on the same curve for 2 or 3 marks, and the sketch is the check on its angles.
traps: Joining the key points with straight lines instead of one smooth curve, which earns the points and loses the shape (Summer 2018 FM1 Q3, Summer 2019 FM1 Q4)
Leaving the axes without a scale, so the values mean nothing (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4, Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Starting a cosine sketch at the origin, which is the sine curve drawn by mistake
Leaving the asymptotes off a tangent sketch, or drawing them at 180° (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Letting the tangent curve touch or cross an asymptote (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Running off the bottom of the grid instead of turning at the minimum (Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Giving 360° as the period of tan x, or 180° as the period of sin x
Changing the sign when using symmetry, which reflects the curve in the x-axis instead of sideways
Stopping at the calculator's angle when the drawn line clearly cuts the curve twice (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4)
A curve drawn upside down (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4)
Too few angles marked along the x-axis (Summer 2019 FM1 Q4)
A sine or cosine shape drawn where the tangent was asked (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)

(a) Sketch the graph of $y = \sin x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.
(b) The line $y = 0.6$ is drawn across it. Use the graph to find both solutions of $\sin x = 0.6$ in that range.

steps.decision: Plot before you draw. The five points fix the whole curve, and they are also what the scheme credits when the curve itself is not smooth enough.

steps.working: Join them with one smooth curve and mark $90$, $180$, $270$, $360$ along the x-axis and $1$ and $-1$ up the y-axis.
steps.decision: The scale is a mark of its own, and it costs four numbers and two more. Straight sides between the turning points throw away the shape mark.

options: Because the curve has to be smooth and the axes have to carry a scale
Because the curve is made of straight lines
Because the y-axis runs from 0 to 360
whyMenu.explain: Shape and scale are the two things a sketch mark is for. Everything else on the page is decoration.

steps.working: Draw the line $y = 0.6$ across the graph. It cuts the curve $2$ times.
steps.decision: Counting the crossings first tells you how many answers to look for, so you cannot stop at one by mistake.
The calculator always gives the angle in the first quadrant here, and that is the one the picture shows on the way up.
The arch is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the second angle is as far past the mirror as the first is short of it. Reading it off the graph gives about $140^\circ$, which agrees.

workedExamples.stem: Sketch the graph of $y = \tan x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, marking the asymptotes and every crossing of the x-axis.

figure.alt: The sketch of y = tan x for x from 0 to 360 degrees: dashed vertical asymptotes at x = 90 and x = 270, three identical branches each rising from left to right, and the crossings of the x-axis at 0, 180 and 360 marked with dots.

steps.working: Asymptotes first: dashed vertical lines at $x = 90$ and $x = 270$.
steps.decision: $\tan x$ is the up measurement divided by the across one, and across is zero at those two angles, so there is no value of the function there at all.

options: Because $\cos x$ is zero there, so the division has no answer
Because the curve has a maximum there
Because the angle is too large
whyMenu.explain: An asymptote marks a missing value, not a turning point. That is why the curve can run off in both directions beside it.

steps.decision: These are the anchors between the asymptotes. Mark them before drawing anything curved.

steps.working: In the strip $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ the curve rises from the origin and climbs steeply towards the dashed line without meeting it.
steps.decision: Steeply towards, never onto. A sketch whose curve touches an asymptote is marked as a misunderstanding of what an asymptote is.

steps.working: Each of the next two strips holds the same branch again, because the pattern repeats every $180^\circ$.
steps.decision: Copy, do not invent. One branch drawn well and repeated twice is a complete answer, and the period is the fact that licenses the copying.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Three identical branches, with dashed asymptotes at $x = 90$ and $x = 270$ and crossings at $0^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $360^\circ$

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new work, so answer from what you already know.
In a right-angled triangle, which ratio is $\sin \theta$?

options.feedback: That is the one. It is also why the sine curve never leaves the strip between -1 and 1: the opposite side can never be longer than the hypotenuse.
That is cosine. The two are easy to swap, and swapping them is what makes a sketch start in the wrong place.
That is tangent, which has no hypotenuse in it at all and so is not trapped between -1 and 1.

items.stem: A curve passes through the point where $x = 4$ and $y = -3$. How are those coordinates written?

options.feedback: Across first, then up or down. Every coordinate answer in this topic is written the same way.
The two numbers are right and they are the wrong way round. The x-value always comes first.
The order here is right. Brackets are how a pair is written, and a mark scheme asking for coordinates expects them.

items.stem: On a calculator set to degrees, what is $\cos 60^\circ$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: reading a trigonometric value in degrees

options.feedback: If your calculator gives something else, it is in radians, and every answer in Unit 1 would come out wrong.
The angle goes in and a ratio comes out, and for cosine that ratio is always between −1 and 1.
That is cos 60 in radians. Set the calculator to degrees before you start.

items.stem: Which curve passes through the point $(0, 1)$?
items.skill: Tell the sine and cosine curves apart

options.feedback: Cosine starts at its maximum, so it is at 1 when the angle is zero.
$\sin 0^\circ = 0$, so the sine curve starts at the origin and climbs from there.
$\tan 0^\circ = 0$ as well, so the tangent curve also starts on the axis.

items.stem: What is the period of $y = \tan x$?
items.skill: Recall the period of each curve

options.feedback: Half the period of the other two. One branch, then the same branch again.
$360^\circ$ is the period of sine and cosine. The tangent curve has already repeated once by then.
$90^\circ$ is the gap from a crossing to an asymptote, which is half a branch rather than a whole one.

items.stem: Where is the asymptote of $y = \tan x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$?
items.skill: Place the asymptotes of the tangent curve

options.feedback: cos x = 0 at 90°, so tan x has no value there: the curve climbs beside the dashed line on one side and starts far below it on the other.
At 180° tan x = 0: the curve crosses the axis there. The asymptote is where cos x = 0, at 90°.
At 45° tan x = 1, a point on the curve. The asymptote is where cos x = 0, at 90°.

items.stem: A sketch of $y = \sin x$ has all five key points plotted correctly, joined by straight lines. How is it marked?
items.skill: Know what the shape mark is for

options.text: The points earn their mark; the shape mark is lost
options.feedback: Examiners have said this for several series running. Joining the points in one smooth pass is the whole difference.

options.text: Full marks, because the points are right
options.feedback: The shape is a separate mark, and straight sides between the turning points are what it is checking for.
Positive marking credits the right values. Only the shape mark goes.

items.skill: Use the symmetry of the sine curve

options.feedback: 180 − 25 = 155: the two angles mirror about 90° on the arch above the axis, so the value is the same, sign and all.
The mirror about 90° moves along the arch, not across the axis: from 0° to 180° every sine value is positive.
That is cos 25°. The sine rule pairs 25° with 180° − 25° = 155° at the same height.

items.stem: The sine curve is drawn for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ and a horizontal line is drawn at $y = 0.4$. How many solutions does that give?
items.skill: Count the solutions a range holds

options.feedback: The line cuts the arch twice, once going up and once coming down, and the rest of the curve stays below it.
The calculator gives one angle. The picture shows the curve reaching that height a second time before the range ends.
There would be four in a range of $720^\circ$, because each period contributes two. This range is one period.

items.stem: On a calculator set to degrees, what is $\sin 30^\circ$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: reading a trigonometric value in degrees

options.feedback: Good. If your calculator gives something else, it is in radians, and every answer in Unit 1 would then come out wrong.
The angle goes in and a ratio comes out. That ratio is always between -1 and 1 for sine.
That is $\sin 30$ in radians. Set the calculator to degrees before you start.

items.stem: Where are the asymptotes of $y = \tan x$ in the range $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$?
items.skill: Place the asymptotes of the tangent curve

options.feedback: Those are the angles where the across measurement is zero, so the division that makes tan has no answer.
Those are the angles where the curve crosses the axis, which is the opposite of a break.
Both of those are crossings as well. The breaks sit halfway between them.

items.skill: Use the symmetry of the sine curve

options.feedback: $180 - 50 = 130$, and the arch is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the height is unchanged.
Changing the sign reflects the curve in the x-axis. The symmetry here is sideways, and it leaves the height where it was.
That is $\cos 50^\circ$. The question stays on the sine curve throughout.

parts.stem:
Write down the period of $y = \sin x$.

Answer ________ °
hints: The period is how far along the x-axis the curve goes before it starts repeating.
parts.workedSolution: One full turn brings the wheel back to where it started, so the sine curve repeats every $360^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: $180^\circ$ is the period of $y = \tan x$. Sine and cosine take a whole turn, so their period is $360^\circ$.
$90^\circ$ is where the first maximum sits, not the period. The period is measured from one maximum to the next.

questions.solutionProgram: period of sin = 360 degrees (one full turn); period of tan = 180

parts.stem:
The graph of $y = \cos x$ is shown above.

Write down the value of $\cos 180^\circ$.

Answer ________
hints: Find $180$ on the x-axis and read straight up or down to the curve.
parts.workedSolution: The cosine curve reaches its minimum at $180^\circ$, so $\cos 180^\circ = -1$.

commonErrors.feedback: $0$ is the value of $\sin 180^\circ$. The cosine curve is at its lowest there, not on the axis.
$1$ is where the cosine curve starts and finishes, at $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. At $180^\circ$ it is exactly the other way round.

parts.stem:
Write down the coordinates of the minimum point of $y = \cos x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: $y = -1$, written as a coordinate pair

hints: The minimum is the lowest point of the curve.
A coordinate pair is written as (x, y).
parts.workedSolution: The lowest point of the cosine curve in this range is at $x = 180$, where $y = -1$, so the minimum point is $(180, -1)$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two numbers are right and they are the wrong way round. A coordinate pair gives the angle first: $(180, -1)$.

questions.solutionProgram: cos(180) = -1; minimum of cos on [0, 360] at (180, -1)

parts.stem: Write down the value of $\tan 180^\circ$.
hints: The tangent curve crosses the x-axis every 180°.
parts.workedSolution: $\tan 180^\circ = \frac{\sin 180^\circ}{\cos 180^\circ}$, which is $\frac{0}{-1} = 0$: the curve crosses the axis there.

parts.stem: Write down the coordinates of the maximum point of $y = \cos x$ for $90^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.
hints: Cosine is lowest at 180° and back at its top a full turn after 0°.
The top at 0° is outside this range.
parts.workedSolution: From $90^\circ$ the cosine curve falls to $-1$ at $180^\circ$ and climbs back to $1$ at $360^\circ$, so the maximum in this range is $(360, 1)$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is cosine's top at 0°, which is outside this range: the range starts at 90°, so its top is the one at 360°.
That is the sine curve's top. Cosine is 0 at 90° and reaches 1 again at 360°.

questions.solutionProgram: a: tan 180° = 0 | b: on 90° ≤ x ≤ 360°, cos x is greatest at 360°: (360, 1)

parts.stem:
The graph of $y = \tan x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ is shown above.

Write down the equations of its two asymptotes.

Answer ________
hints: An asymptote is a line the curve gets closer and closer to without ever reaching it.
Both of them are vertical, so each has an equation of the form x = a number.
parts.workedSolution:
$\tan x$ has no value where the cosine underneath it is zero, and that happens at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ in this range.
So the asymptotes are the vertical lines $x = 90$ and $x = 270$.

commonErrors.feedback: $180^\circ$ is where the tangent curve crosses the axis, not where it breaks. The breaks are a quarter of a turn either side of it.
The values are right and the lines are vertical, so each equation begins $x =$, not $y =$.

questions.solutionProgram: tan undefined where cos x = 0 on [0, 360]: x = 90, 270

Use the symmetry of the curve to write down the value of $\sin 140^\circ$.

scheme.for: using the correct symmetry, $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x$

hints: Sketch the curve and mark $40^\circ$ and $140^\circ$ on it.
The rule here is $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x$.
parts.workedSolution:
$180 - 40 = 140$, and the first arch of the sine curve is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so the two angles sit at the same height on the curve.
Therefore $\sin 140^\circ = 0.64$.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, so the method mark stands. Changing the sign would mean reflecting the curve in the x-axis; the symmetry here reflects it sideways, which leaves the height alone.

Use the graph above to find the smaller solution of $\sin x = 0.6$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: a reading within $5^\circ$ of $36.87$

hints: Drop a line from the first crossing down to the x-axis and read the scale.
parts.workedSolution: The line meets the curve for the first time just before $40^\circ$. Reading down to the axis gives about $37^\circ$, and a calculator confirms $36.87^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the second crossing. This part asks for the smaller of the two, which is the one on the rising part of the curve.

parts.stem:
Use the graph to find the other solution of $\sin x = 0.6$ in the same range.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: reading the second crossing, or using $180 - 36.87$
a reading within $5^\circ$ of $143.13$

hints: The curve comes back down to the same height on the far side of the maximum.
Or use the rule $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x$.
parts.workedSolution:
The second crossing is the mirror image of the first in the line $x = 90^\circ$.
$180 - 36.87 = 143.13$, which agrees with the reading of about $143^\circ$ from the graph.

commonErrors.feedback: $360 - 36.87$ is the cosine rule, and it lands below the axis on this curve. For sine the partner angle is $180^\circ$ minus the first one.

questions.solutionProgram: sin x = 0.6 on [0, 360] -> 36.87, 143.13; wrong second solution route 360 - base = 323.13

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: Every solution on a two-period range from one calculator angle, the symmetry and the period

parts.stem:
The graph of $y = \sin x$ is drawn for $-360^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.
How many solutions does $\sin x = -0.3$ have in this range?

scheme.for: $4$, the crossings of $y = -0.3$ with the curve

hints: Draw the line y = −0.3 across the curve.
How many times does it cut each 360° stretch?
parts.workedSolution: The line $y = -0.3$ cuts the sine curve twice in each $360^\circ$, and the range is two periods long, so there are $4$ solutions.

commonErrors.feedback: That counts one period. The range runs from −360° to 360°, two periods, and the line cuts each of them twice: 4.

parts.stem:
Your calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(-0.3) = -17.5^\circ$, to 1 decimal place.
Use the symmetry and the period of the curve to find all the solutions of $\sin x = -0.3$ for $-360^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, each to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: a second solution from the symmetry of the curve, such as $-180 + 17.5 = -162.5$
three of the four solutions

hints: The arch below the axis from −180° to 0° is symmetrical about −90°.
Then add 360° to each angle you have, keeping only those in the range.
parts.workedSolution:
The arch from $-180^\circ$ to $0^\circ$ mirrors about $-90^\circ$, so $-17.5^\circ$ pairs with $-180 + 17.5 = -162.5^\circ$.
Adding $360^\circ$ to each: $342.5^\circ$ and $197.5^\circ$, both in range.
So $x = -162.5^\circ$, $-17.5^\circ$, $197.5^\circ$ or $342.5^\circ$.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

context.setting: A cosine sketch and the equation it is then used to solve

parts.stem: Sketch the graph of $y = \cos x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, marking the scale on both axes.

rubric: One smooth curve, with no straight stretches between the turning points
A scale on both axes: $1$ and $-1$ up the vertical one, the angles under the horizontal one
The maximum and the minimum at the right angles, drawn as turning points rather than corners

scheme.for: the correct shape: one smooth curve starting at its maximum, with turning points and no straight sides
the scale shown: $1$ and $-1$ up the vertical axis, with $90$, $180$, $270$ and $360$ written under the horizontal one

hints: Plot the five key points first, then join them in one smooth pass.
Cosine starts at its highest point, not at the origin.
parts.workedSolution:
Plot $(0, 1)$, $(90, 0)$, $(180, -1)$, $(270, 0)$ and $(360, 1)$.
Join them with a single smooth curve, flat at the top and flat at the bottom, and write $90$, $180$, $270$, $360$ along the x-axis and $1$ and $-1$ up the y-axis.

parts.stem:
The line $y = -0.8$ is drawn across your sketch.

How many solutions does $\cos x = -0.8$ have for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$?

Answer ________
hints: The line sits below the axis, so look at the part of the curve that dips below it.
parts.workedSolution: The cosine curve dips below $y = -0.8$ once, between $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$, so the line cuts it $2$ times.

commonErrors.feedback: The curve goes down through that height and comes back up through it, so it meets the line twice. Counting the calculator's single angle is the commonest loss on this topic.

parts.stem:
Use your sketch to find the smaller solution of $\cos x = -0.8$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: a value within $5^\circ$ of $143.13$

hints: A calculator gives this one directly.
parts.workedSolution: A calculator gives the first angle as $143.13^\circ$, which is about $143^\circ$ on the sketch.

parts.stem:
Find the other solution of $\cos x = -0.8$ in the same range.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: $360 - 143.13$, or the second crossing read from the sketch
a value within $5^\circ$ of $216.87$

hints: The cosine curve is symmetrical about the middle of the range.
Take the first angle away from $360^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution: The cosine curve is symmetrical about $x = 180^\circ$, so the second angle is $360 - 143.13 = 216.87^\circ$, which is about $217^\circ$ on the sketch.

commonErrors.feedback: $180$ minus the first angle is the sine rule. On the cosine curve the mirror is at $180^\circ$ itself, so the partner is $360^\circ$ minus the first angle.

resources: Scientific calculator
Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

emphasis: the tangent curve and its asymptotes

context.setting: The tangent curve over a range that crosses zero

parts.stem: Sketch the graph of $y = \tan x$ for $-180^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$, showing the asymptotes clearly.

rubric: Three branches, each rising from bottom left to top right, with no straight stretches
Dashed vertical asymptotes at $x = -90$ and $x = 90$ that the curve approaches but never meets
Crossings marked at $-180$, $0$ and $180$, and the angles written along the x axis

scheme.for: three branches of the correct shape, each rising from bottom left to top right
dashed asymptotes at $x = -90$ and $x = 90$ that the curve approaches but never meets

hints: Draw the asymptotes first, then the curve between and beyond them.
The curve crosses the axis at $-180^\circ$, $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.
parts.workedSolution:
Draw dashed vertical lines at $x = -90$ and $x = 90$.
The curve crosses the x-axis at $-180^\circ$, $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, and in each of the three strips it climbs from far below on the left to far above on the right without touching either dashed line.

parts.stem:
Write down the period of $y = \tan x$.

Answer ________ °
hints: Measure from one branch to the identical branch beside it.
parts.workedSolution: Every branch of the tangent curve is a copy of the one before it, and the branches sit $180^\circ$ apart, so the period is $180^\circ$.

commonErrors.feedback: $360^\circ$ is the period of sine and cosine. The tangent curve has already repeated itself once by then.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $x$, strictly between $-180^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, at which your sketch crosses the x-axis and is also a point of the curve $y = \sin x$.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: recognising that both curves pass through the origin

hints: $\tan x$ is zero at $-180^\circ$, $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.
$\sin x$ is also zero at all three, so look for the one that is a point of both curves and lies strictly between the ends of the range.
parts.workedSolution:
$\tan x = 0$ at $-180^\circ$, $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, and $\sin x$ is zero at each of them too.
The range is open at its ends here, so the value strictly inside it is $x = 0$.

commonErrors.feedback: $90^\circ$ is an asymptote of the tangent curve, so there is no point of the curve there at all.

questions.solutionProgram: tan zeros on [-180, 180]: -180, 0, 180; asymptotes at -90, 90; period 180

findTheMistake.stem: Órlaith is told that $\sin 50^\circ = 0.77$ and asked for the value of $\sin 130^\circ$. Her working:
studentWorking: 130 is past the maximum, so the curve is on its way down
180 - 50 = 130, so the two angles are a pair
Going down means the value is negative
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are exactly right: $130^\circ$ does sit on the falling part of the arch, and it is the mirror image of $50^\circ$ in the line $x = 90^\circ$.
Line 3 confuses falling with negative. Between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ the whole arch sits above the axis, so every value there is positive however steeply the curve is dropping.
The curve only goes below the axis after $180^\circ$, and $130^\circ$ is comfortably short of that.
correction: The mirror line x = 90 leaves the height unchanged
findTheMistake.feedback: The method mark is safe: spotting the pair is the part that is worth thinking about, and Órlaith spotted it. Sketch the arch and mark both angles on it before writing the value down, and the sign settles itself.

findTheMistake.stem: Cormac was asked to use the graph of $y = \tan x$ to solve $\tan x = 2.5$ for $-180^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$, to 1 decimal place. His working:
studentWorking: The line y = 2.5 cuts the branch through the origin at 68.2
So x = 68.2 is the only solution
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 stops at the calculator's angle: the branch from −180° to −90° also climbs past 2.5, and since tangent repeats every 180° it does so at 68.2 − 180 = −111.8°.
findTheMistake.feedback: Before writing the answer, count the crossings on the sketch: every branch that reaches the line gives a solution, and tangent's branches are 180° apart.

prompts.prompt: Give the five key points of $y = \sin x$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
Give the five key points of $y = \cos x$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
What is the period of each of the three curves?
prompts.answer: Sine and cosine repeat every 360 degrees; tangent repeats every 180 degrees.

prompts.prompt: Where are the asymptotes of $y = \tan x$, and what does the curve do at one?
prompts.answer: At 90 and 270 degrees, and at every angle 180 degrees from those. The curve gets closer and closer to the line without ever touching it.

prompts.prompt: A sketch has every key point plotted correctly. What else does the mark scheme want?
prompts.answer: One smooth curve with no straight sides, and a scale written on both axes.

prompts.prompt: How do you find a second solution of $\sin x = k$ once your calculator has given you the first?
prompts.answer: Take the first angle away from 180 degrees, or read the second crossing off the sketch: the arch is symmetrical about 90 degrees.

prompts.prompt: Why is $\cos(360^\circ - x) = \cos x$ rather than $\cos(180^\circ - x) = \cos x$?
prompts.answer: Because the cosine curve is symmetrical about 180 degrees, so 0 pairs with 360. The 180 minus rule belongs to sine, whose mirror is at 90 degrees.

prompts.prompt: What does the curve $y = \tan x$ do near an asymptote?
prompts.answer: It gets closer and closer to the line but never touches it.

prompts.prompt: Which line is the first arch of $y = \sin x$ symmetrical about?
What is the period of $y = \tan x$?

findings.wentWrong: Correct points but sides drawn too straight; marks only for the points.
Curves too straight between max and min; too few values marked - the x-axis needs -90, 0, 90, 180, 270, 360 and the y-axis +1 and -1.
findings.rule: Mark the key angles and the values plus and minus 1.

findings.wentWrong: No scales on the axes; some inverted the graph.
findings.rule: Sine starts at the origin going up; label the axes.

findings.wentWrong: The turning points at plus and minus 180 were not shown - sketches ran straight off below -1; the y-axis had no scale.
findings.rule: Cosine turns at plus or minus 180 with value -1.

findings.wentWrong: Asymptotes were omitted or placed at 180; curves touched or crossed them; the x-axis was unlabelled; some drew sine-like shapes.
findings.rule: Tan has asymptotes at 90 and 270; the curve approaches them but never touches.

insight.ruleToRemember: Sketch a smooth curve with the key angles and plus or minus 1 marked; tan needs vertical asymptotes at 90 and 270 that the curve never touches.

checks.detail: Every printed value comes from Math.sin, Math.cos or Math.tan in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/lib.mjs, rounded once for printing. Key points sin (0, 0) (90, 1) (180, 0) (270, -1) (360, 0); cos (0, 1) (90, 0) (180, -1) (270, 0) (360, 1); tan zeros 0, 180, 360 with asymptotes at 90 and 270. Every symmetry pair was checked to 9 decimal places before it was printed (sin 25/155 = 0.42; sin 40/140 = 0.64; sin 50/130 = 0.77; cos 70/290 = 0.34; cos 35/325 = 0.82; tan 32/212 = 0.62). Readings: sin x = 0.6 gives 36.87 and 143.13; cos x = -0.8 gives 143.13 and 216.87; tan x = 2 gives 63.43 and 243.43. Distractors come from the routes in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/routes.mjs (baseAngleOnly, wrongSecondSolution, a reflection in the x-axis), never typed by hand, and verify-published.mjs re-executes each one against the published JSON.

checks.detail: Marked back through the app's own engines (src/components/items/mark.ts onto numeric.ts, algebra.ts, points.ts and text-marking.ts) by scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/check-marking.mts: 1230 assertions over the four bundles' 82 question parts, 46 note gates and 35 note figures, all passing. The note's shape is checked too: a hero block first with three lines and a lede inside 60 words, a gate after every video, a visual in every numbered section, a recap card, and a gate inside the closing panel. Error routes re-executed against the published JSON by scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/verify-published.mjs: 75 routes, 98 published common errors (49 numeric, 49 algebraic, 14 of those re-derived as a structural error applied to the part's own published answer), no unexplained value and none typed by hand. In this bundle: 10 questions over 17 parts, 11 gates, 10 note figures, longest teaching stretch 137 words and longest closing-panel stretch 205.
